Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 40-year-old woman with 48-hour history of progressive wheeze and dyspnea beginning after heavy dust exposure.  
• Past childhood asthma; keeps salbutamol inhaler; intermittent hay fever.  
• No chest pain, dizziness, fever, or other systemic symptoms.  
• No objective observations yet taken.

Working diagnosis  
• Acute asthma exacerbation precipitated by dust/allergen exposure.

Differential considerations (consistent with DDx)  
• Acute allergic reaction with lower-airway involvement.  
• Viral upper/lower respiratory tract infection (early bronchitis).  
• Pulmonary embolism—low likelihood but considered.

Management plan  
• Advise patient to attend local GP/clinic today for:  
  – Pulse oximetry, peak-flow measurement, and respiratory examination.  
  – Consider short course of oral corticosteroid if moderate/severe obstruction confirmed.  
  – Initiate or update reliever (SABA) inhaler prescription and teach proper technique.  
  – Trial non-sedating antihistamine (OTC) pending assessment.  
• Provide referral letter via app to facilitate in-person review.  
• Escalate to emergency care if worsening breathlessness, inability to speak full sentences, or reduced oxygen saturation.

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification:  Counseled on allergen avoidance (dust), appropriate inhaler use, and importance of timely medical review—further education deferred to in-person visit.

- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled:  To be arranged after GP assessment; urgent review if symptoms worsen.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Asthma exacerbation (High) – Temporal link to dust, childhood asthma history, classic nocturnal wheeze.  
2. Acute allergic reaction to dust mite antigen (Medium) – Allergen exposure and hay-fever background; lacks systemic allergy signs.  
3. Viral acute bronchitis (Low-Medium) – Possible but no cough/fever and clear non-infective trigger.
